title: Lyra Retail — Latency Spectrum Fieldbook
content:
Purpose:
This fieldbook captures a series of benchmarking experiments run for the Lyra Retail POC. The goal was to characterize latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), sustainable throughput, and per-token cost across a representative set of request shapes and deployment configurations. It is intentionally iterative and includes raw observations, anomalies, and recommended next steps for the customer proposal.

Context and customer ask:
Lyra Retail needs sub-150ms p95 for simple search-assist queries and sub-700ms p95 for multi-turn recommendation prompts at 1.5k QPS peak during promotions. Cost sensitivity: they asked for a rough USD/month estimate for steady-state 1M queries/day (mixed size) and an outline of scaling behavior during 10x promo burst.

Testbed summary:
- Date range: 2028-01-09 -> 2028-01-12 (this doc summarizes follow-ups run 2028-01-18)
- Models: small->medium recommended variants: open-llm-retail-7b (FP16), open-llm-retail-7b-q4_0 (int8-like), open-llm-retail-13b (FP16)
- Hardware: g4dn-equivalent 1xA100-80GB (single-GPU) and 4xA100-80GB pooled nodes (dedicated), and an edge-proxy host (cpu) used to simulate network egress and TLS overhead.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v3.8.1, kernel-selection enabled, and KV prefix caching experiment branch (kv-prefix-experiments-2028).
- Workload generator: internal harness (bench-gen v2.3) with mixed arrival patterns: steady Poisson baseline, 10x sudden promotion burst (10s ramp), and microburst pattern (many small concurrent fanout requests).
- Observability: per-request traces, token billing counters, GPU utilization (nvidia-smi sampled at 1s), runtime queue lengths, and kernel selection logs.

Workload shapes tested:
- SEARCH-SHORT: 12-token prompt, single completion ~20 tokens (typical product search assist)
- REC-CHAT: 120-token context, multi-turn 2-step completion ~120 tokens (recommendation + followup)
- ANALYTICS: 400-token prompt, longer generation ~300 tokens (batch offline style, lower latency SLO)
- MIXED-MAIN: weighted mix (70% SEARCH-SHORT, 25% REC-CHAT, 5% ANALYTICS) to represent production mix for cost numbers.

Scenarios (each run repeated 5x to capture variance):
A) Single-GPU baseline, FP16 model, no batching, cold start every 10s (simulate low concurrency gateway)
B) Single-GPU, FP16, dynamic batching enabled (max latency target 100ms), warm steady load
C) 4xGPU dedicated pool, autoscale off, batching + KV prefix caching on
D) 4xGPU, q4 quantized model (reduced memory), batching aggressive (max batch 512 tokens), fallback policy to FP16 when saturated
E) Edge-proxy enabled (adds 8-12ms TLS + 4-6ms cold DNS) to measure client-observed latency

Key metrics collected (examples summarized below):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 (ms) measured at request completion (wall-clock including network emulation when edge-proxy enabled)
- Throughput: successful req/s sustained over 60s windows and 5-min windows
- GPU utilization: mean and peak over experiment
- Cost estimate: token cost model using Redwood hosted list: FP16 $0.00002/token gen, q4 $0.000012/token gen + fixed infra amortized per-hour estimates for dedicated pool

Summarized results (selected numbers; each value is median of 5 runs):
Scenario A (single-GPU, no batching, cold starts):
- SEARCH-SHORT: p50 42ms, p95 190ms, p99 420ms; sustained throughput 160 req/s; GPU util avg 18% (spiky)
- REC-CHAT: p50 180ms, p95 780ms, p99 1.9s; sustained throughput 28 req/s; GPU util avg 40%
- MIXED-MAIN overall: p95 320ms, p99 950ms; cost estimate ~USD 26k/mo for 1M queries/day (dominant token gen cost + single-GPU reserved infra)

Scenario B (single-GPU, dynamic batching):
- SEARCH-SHORT: p50 55ms, p95 82ms, p99 210ms; sustained throughput 420 req/s; GPU util avg 56%
- REC-CHAT: p50 210ms, p95 420ms, p99 920ms; sustained throughput 160 req/s; GPU util avg 68%
- MIXED-MAIN: p95 150ms, p99 440ms; cost estimate ~USD 14k/mo for 1M queries/day (batching reduces per-token compute by ~40%)
- Notes: batching improved throughput significantly but increased p50 for short requests due to batching hold-time. With dynamic batch-timeouts tuned to 25ms p95 target for SEARCH-SHORT we hit p95~95ms.

Scenario C (4xGPU dedicated, batching + KV prefix caching):
- SEARCH-SHORT: p50 18ms, p95 48ms, p99 120ms; sustained throughput 2.5k req/s; GPU util avg 72% across pool
- REC-CHAT: p50 95ms, p95 290ms, p99 640ms; sustained throughput 680 req/s; GPU util avg 80%
- MIXED-MAIN: p95 70ms, p99 220ms; cost estimate (dedicated pool amortized) ~USD 58k/mo for capacity to sustain 1M queries/day with headroom for 10x bursts (note: includes dedicated infra surcharge and premium SLA)
- Observations: KV prefix caching reduced token compute by 18% on MIXED-MAIN and cut p95 for REC-CHAT by ~30% (fewer tokens computed due to cached prefixes).

Scenario D (4xGPU with q4 quantized model + aggressive batching + fallback):
- SEARCH-SHORT: p50 16ms, p95 42ms, p99 110ms; sustained throughput 3.1k req/s; GPU util avg 68%
- REC-CHAT: p50 110ms, p95 340ms, p99 820ms; sustained throughput 840 req/s; GPU util avg 72%
- MIXED-MAIN: p95 82ms, p99 260ms; cost estimate ~USD 33k/mo (significant per-token savings from quantized path)
- Failure mode observed: under extreme microburst (many concurrent short requests) fallback policy triggered more than desired — config needs better backoff to avoid oscillation between q4 and FP16 when queue latencies spike.

Scenario E (edge-proxy enabled):
- Additive client-observed latency: +12ms median, +28ms p95 (TLS and small routing jitter). Real SLOs should account for ~30ms of network+proxy overhead in worst-case regions.

Comparative takeaways:
- Batching is the single most powerful lever for cost and throughput; it trades p50 for higher throughput. For SEARCH-SHORT we must tune batching timeouts aggressively (<=25ms) to meet sub-150ms p95 targets while still capturing batching gains for REC-CHAT.
- KV prefix caching yields consistent reductions for conversational/rec workloads where context shares prefixes across requests (roughly 15-20% token compute reduction observed).
- Quantization (q4) lowers per-token cost and increases throughput; however, it introduces variability when fallback logic toggles during microbursts — we need hysteresis and queue-aware logic.
- Dedicated 4xGPU pools achieve the best tail-latency with headroom for bursts, but their amortized monthly cost is higher; the right trade depends on Lyra's willingness to buy reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go.

Anomalies and open questions:
- We saw intermittent kernel-selection thrash on 13b model when sequence-length distribution swung during REC-CHAT bursts (kernel switch logs showed 3 switches in <500ms). Need runtime team help to trace kernel selection heuristics and whether warm kernels persist across requests.
- Observed a reproducible spike in p99 around 17:03 local time during long runs; correlates with NVLink peer sync observed in node logs. Is there an infra-level maintenance job or crontab tied to that time on the test cluster?
- Billing model uncertainty: the customer asked for committed-side discounts; current cost numbers assume list pricing. We should prepare 3 pricing scenarios: pay-as-you-go, committed 12mo, and enterprise reserved with support.

Immediate recommendations for Lyra Retail POC proposal:
1) For strict p95 <150ms for SEARCH-SHORT at baseline QPS, use single-GPU FP16 with dynamic batching tuned to 25ms max hold-time and an edge proxy placed in same region. This gives acceptable cost (~USD14k/mo) and meets SLO for non-peak windows.
2) For promotion windows (10x bursts), provide a dedicated 4xGPU pool as overflow capacity with automatic routing policy. Use KV prefix caching and q4 quant for the overflow path. Keep aggressive hysteresis on fallback to avoid oscillation.
3) Highlight a two-path SLA in proposal: baseline (hosted shared pool) + reserved surge pool (dedicated) with clear cost delta in the one-pager.
4) Action item for runtime: add kernel-selection trace correlation with request IDs and add a small delay before kernel switch to prevent rapid thrashing.
5) Action item for infra: investigate the 17:03 node-level spike and ensure no cron/scheduled job interferes with production-like testbeds.

Next steps and experiments to run (owner tags):
- Marco: run longer 24-hour stability test with realistic traffic shape and measure p99 drift (due 2028-01-25).
- Leah: prototype fallback hysteresis (hold-off 200ms after fallback trigger) and re-run microburst tests (due 2028-01-22).
- Omar: generate customer-ready cost scenarios (payg / 12mo commit / enterprise reserved) with sensitivity to token size mix and export as spreadsheet (due 2028-01-23).

Appendix (quick notes and shorthand):
- bench-gen commands used: bench-gen --profile lyra-mixed-2028 --qps 1500 --burst 15000 --pattern promo-ramp
- runtime flags: --batcher-timeout-ms 25 --kv-prefix-cache=true --quant-fallback=hysteresis:200ms (prototype)
- quick links: JIRA-ENG-4521 (Lyra POC), GH PR 231 (kv-prefix-experiments), confluence link above

Notes to self: this doc is a working artifact for the proposal deck. Keep raw CSVs in /shared/bench-exports/lyra/2028-01 for audit. We should convert key graphs to the customer-facing one-pager and include the two-path cost table (baseline vs dedicated surge).

Unresolved for proposal language: decide whether to frame dedicated surge as "reserved capacity" (higher up-front cost, stable latency) or "burstable reserved" (lower baseline commit + short-term burstable credits). Need pricing input from sales before finalizing the one-pager.

-- Asha M. (fieldbook draft)
